title: T. rex Was Warm Like You! Scientists Take a Dinosaur's Temperature
summary:
Imagine touching a T. rex and finding out it feels almost as warm as you do. Scientists just did something that seemed impossible: they took the temperature of a dinosaur that died 66 million years ago.

The answer? About 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 Celsius). That's about the same as a human. A lizard today is usually only 82 to 86 degrees.

How do you take a temperature from a fossil? The secret is in the teeth. Inside tooth enamel, tiny chemicals called isotopes bond together. More bonds form when it's cool, fewer when it's warm. So the tooth works like a tiny ancient thermometer.

Researchers at UCLA used a dental drill to collect a little enamel from two teeth of "Thomas the T. rex," a famous skeleton at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. They turned the powder into a gas and measured it with a special machine.

"No one's been able to make a temperature measurement like this before," said Robert Eagle, a scientist on the team.

Why does it matter? A warm body means T. rex was an active hunter, not a slow sunbather. It could even live in cold places like Alaska. Not bad for a giant reptile!
why_it_matters: Knowing that dinosaurs were warm like us changes how we picture them — as fast, busy animals instead of slow ones — and it shows kids that clever science can answer questions that once seemed impossible.

background_read: T. rex lived about 66 million years ago, at the end of the age of dinosaurs, and nobody has ever seen one alive — scientists can only study the bones and teeth it left behind.
Most reptiles alive today, like lizards and snakes, are cold-blooded: their bodies stay about as warm as the air around them, so they often sit in the sun to heat up.

The team works at UCLA (a big university in California), and the famous T. rex skeleton they studied is kept at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (a museum in Los Angeles where dinosaur bones are displayed).
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at UCLA, including Robert Eagle, a scientist on the team, and 'Thomas the T. rex' at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
WHAT: They measured the body temperature of a dinosaur that died 66 million years ago and found it was about 97°F (36°C), close to a human's
WHERE: The enamel came from two teeth of a T. rex skeleton in Los Angeles, and the measuring was done by the researchers at UCLA in California
WHY: A warm body means T. rex was an active hunter, not a slow sunbather, and could even have lived in cold places like Alaska

perspectives.description: The team says no one has been able to make a temperature measurement like this before, so it is a brand-new way to study animals that died millions of years ago.
Some researchers may ask whether two teeth from one dinosaur are enough, and whether the chemicals in teeth always work the same way in every fossil.
People who love dinosaurs get a new picture of T. rex as a fast, active hunter that might even have lived in chilly places like Alaska.
